hero.headline: Fertilizer ban begins Monday in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties
hero.body:
Starting June 30, residents across Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties will need to stop applying fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen. The ban extends through the rainy season as a measure to minimize nutrient-rich runoff that flows into local waterways. Officials say this runoff can trigger harmful algae blooms in environmentally sensitive areas including the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River.

Jordan Skaggs, who works with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, explained the purpose behind the restriction. The ban is designed to reduce nutrient pollution during months when heavy rainfall increases the likelihood of fertilizer washing into nearby water systems. According to Skaggs, algae blooms stemming from excess nutrients can have serious consequences. "It can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife," he said. Beyond blocking sunlight, these blooms become problematic at higher concentrations. "At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that can affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health."

For residents looking for ways to maintain their gardens and landscaping during the ban period, composting offers a practical solution. Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, advocates for this approach. Ricketts noted that composting does not require complicated equipment or significant expense. "It can be like a small trash can," Ricketts said. "That is the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape." By composting organic materials, homeowners can create their own nutrient source while simultaneously reducing chemical runoff during the critical rainy season.

The fertilizer restrictions apply uniformly across all three counties on the Treasure Coast, ensuring a coordinated approach to protecting regional water quality. Residents who need more information about permitted alternatives or have specific questions about the ban should contact the University of Florida's St. Lucie County Extension office. Officials encourage people to plan ahead and prepare alternative landscaping methods before the June 30 start date to avoid any disruptions to their yard maintenance routines.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds receives death threats during Florida gubernatorial campaign, calls for responsible political rhetoric
cards.teaser: Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds disclosed Friday that he has received multiple death threats while running for the Republican nomination in the Au.
cards.body:
Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds is speaking out about threats on his life as he runs for the Republican nomination in the August primary. The Naples Republican, in his third term in Congress, faced one threat on social media last month after resharing President Donald Trump's endorsement in the governor's race. A second person called Donalds' district office making similar threats, saying he was going to blow up the entire office. "Somebody just flat out said they were going to kill me," Donalds told radio host Mark Levin on Friday.

Donalds cited the assassination of conservative Charlie Kirk last year as an example of what happens when political opponents are demonized and not treated as human beings. He said that demonizing someone to the point where they are portrayed as going to destroy Florida gives an opening to somebody with real mental health issues to attempt violence. While considering himself a free speech absolutist, Donalds stressed the importance of being mindful of how things are being said to avoid creating an environment where someone takes it upon themselves to take another person's life. Donalds said the incident strengthened his resolve to work hard to be the state's next governor and to keep Florida free as the preeminent conservative and common sense state in America. He remains undeterred by the threats and expresses confidence in his position in the race to succeed Ron DeSantis.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island erosion threatens to split island at Peck Lake, state report warns
cards.teaser: Nearly the entire coastline of Jupiter Island is critically eroded, with the ocean threatening to breach the island at Peck Lake and split it in half, according to a new state report.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. A storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. The erosion threatens the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, along with Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge and St. Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said over 33 threatened and endangered species live in those areas.

Jupiter Island continues fighting erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project, dumping enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said about $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment every year. Field warned that if funding for beach renourishment ever goes away, the coastline of Florida will change very quickly. He said if the island were to breach, repairs could require massive state and federal investment.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance closes within hours as demand outpaces funding
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program receives about 600 applications in the first couple hours each month, far exceeding available resources.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Community Services Department has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding for its Emergency Rental Assistance Program, but demand far outweighs available resources. The department receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month and currently has about 800 applications in the queue. Applications open at the beginning of each month but fill quickly, with the county typically receiving about 600 applications within the first couple of hours. At the time of reporting, the county's assistance portal was marked closed due to high demand. Program director Dr. James Green urged anyone in need to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability. Green attributed the recent surge in applications to rising costs of living, including housing, gas, and food.

According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month. Joanne Bromfield, who recently moved to West Palm Beach from Tampa, switched from a 12-year career as an educator to real estate in hopes of earning higher income to afford rent. Green said preventing homelessness depends on everyone and called on people with extra housing to partner with the county to help neighbors in need. For those unable to access the county's program, 211 offers another resource available 24/7 to connect residents with nonprofits and other assistance programs in the area.

cards.headline: Florida man arrested after chasing children on bikes with baseball bat
cards.teaser: A Florida man was taken into custody after allegedly chasing children riding bikes while wielding a baseball bat.
cards.body:
A Florida man faces charges after police say he chased children on bikes while armed with a baseball bat. The incident prompted calls to law enforcement and led to his arrest.

Authorities responded to reports of a man threatening children in the area. Witnesses reported seeing the suspect pursuing the youngsters while carrying the bat.

The man was arrested following the incident. Police are investigating the circumstances that led to the confrontation with the children.

cards.headline: Florida could ban Fourth of July fireworks statewide due to drought conditions
cards.teaser: State leaders are considering banning fireworks for the Fourth of July's 250th anniversary celebration as drought conditions across Florida worsen beyond 1998 levels.
cards.body:
Florida's Fourth of July celebrations could look dramatically different this year as state leaders weigh whether to ban fireworks due to severe drought conditions. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services says this year's drought is even more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide fireworks ban was imposed. The entire state of Florida is at least abnormally dry, with areas including Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing moderate to extreme drought conditions.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson warned in May that if drought conditions persist through the Fourth of July, a ban is likely. "You could put the entire state on fire in evening all over the state all at one time," Simpson said, noting the potential impact of hundreds of thousands of people using fireworks simultaneously. Simpson acknowledged the significance of the 250th celebration of American independence but urged residents to consider alternatives. At Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, owner Bill Murphy reported increased customer activity ahead of the holiday but said the store remains cautiously optimistic, noting there is plenty of rain in the forecast. The Department of Agriculture said a fireworks ban would be a last resort.

cards.headline: Florida voters divided on property tax ballot measure requiring 60% approval
cards.teaser: Florida voters will decide this November whether to raise the homestead exemption and roll back property taxes, but how much cities and counties would lose remains unknown.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide this November whether to raise the homestead exemption to roll back property taxes, a proposal that requires 60% approval to pass. A similar measure failed in 2018. How much money cities and counties would lose under the plan remains unclear, as does where budget cuts would fall if voters approve it.

Support for the measure split along housing status. Brian Edington, a West Palm Beach homeowner, backs the idea because it benefits people who permanently live in Florida. He said he is comfortable with local governments spending less and pointed to his neighborhood's trash services as an example, noting that once-weekly pickup would be adequate instead of twice weekly. However, renters expressed skepticism. One resident along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach said property owners would raise rent on renters to offset the tax savings. Rosabella Olivares, a shopper in West Palm Beach, expressed concern about reduced funding, saying "everything is expensive now."

cards.headline: Home security camera leads to arrest during burglary at Port St. Lucie apartment
cards.teaser: Sebastian Thibodeau was arrested Thursday after a resident's security camera captured him burglarizing an apartment at Sanctuary Apartments at Winterlakes in real time.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie resident's home security camera caught a burglary in real-time Thursday afternoon at Sanctuary Apartments at Winterlakes in the 5400 block of NW Moorehen Trail. Around 3:38 p.m., the apartment resident received a motion alert from his security system while away from home. Upon checking his live camera feed, he spotted a masked man inside his apartment. The resident activated his camera's audible siren, causing the suspect to leave briefly before returning to tamper with the camera itself.

Multiple witnesses saw the suspect flee the victim's apartment and enter a neighboring unit in the same building. When Port St. Lucie Police arrived, they found clear signs of forced entry, including damage to the front door and door frame. Officers established a perimeter while the SWAT team was called to assist. After repeated announcements, Sebastian Thibodeau, 36, exited the apartment and surrendered without incident. Investigators collected surveillance footage from doorbell cameras throughout the complex that captured a man matching the suspect's description before and after the burglary. A watch valued at approximately $300 was stolen during the incident. Thibodeau was charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling and transported to the St. Lucie County jail.

cards.headline: Florida Supreme Court adopts new AI courtroom rules taking effect June 15
cards.teaser: Florida attorneys and self-represented litigants will be required to certify that what they cite in court exists and is accurate under new rules addressing AI misuse.
cards.body:
The Florida Supreme Court recently adopted new rules requiring attorneys and self-represented litigants to certify that what they cite in court exists and is accurate. The rules take effect June 15 and address what many in the legal and AI field have described as a growing crisis: the misuse of artificial intelligence in courtrooms. Sanctions for violations could range from a public reprimand to fines and even suspension. Federal Judge William Matthewman, chief magistrate for the Southern District of Florida, said fake evidence, fabricated facts and bogus case law have become so much of a concern that the state's highest court was compelled to act. "Unfortunately, I see it getting worse before it gets better," Matthewman said, adding that while the Florida Supreme Court's order will help in Florida, he has seen the problem growing over the last couple of years.

In Polk County, an attorney representing the Polk County School District in an ongoing lawsuit over school bus cameras was recently chastised after a judge discovered fabricated facts and cited cases that don't exist were filed as part of a motion to dismiss. The attorney said he used ChatGPT as a drafting and research aid but admitted there was no excuse for his failure to verify before filing. A school district spokesperson said they take accuracy and integrity in legal proceedings seriously and are reviewing whether the attorney will be eligible for contracted services again.

hero.headline: Florida shark diving operators fight federal feeding ban they say could devastate Treasure Coast tourism
hero.body:
A proposed federal ban on shark feeding off Florida's coast has triggered intense pushback from the state's shark diving industry, which argues the measure will harm conservation-focused tourism businesses without meaningfully improving public safety. Known as the Safe Florida Seas Act, H.R. 3831 has passed the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, though it includes an exception for harvesting operations. Proponents of the bill contend it represents a practical safety step to reduce encounters between humans and sharks.

Dive operators say the legislation unfairly singles out their sector, which consists largely of small businesses and nonprofits centered on education and responsible wildlife encounters, while ignoring practices used in commercial fishing. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, points out that Congress has not sought input from the diving industry about their operations or data. The operators emphasize that their methods differ significantly from fishing practices. They deploy bait underwater during dives rather than chumming at the surface, a technique they say is less likely to train sharks to seek food near boats. Commercial fishing operations, by contrast, can discharge hundreds of gallons of chum at the surface. Campbell stressed that the industry welcomes accountability and simply wants the opportunity to present evidence and explain their practices.

The bill references Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as a model. However, Florida operators and some researchers argue Hawaii's experience actually serves as a cautionary tale. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, notes that shark diving in Florida maintains a "near perfect safety record" for customers. Since Hawaii implemented its ban, industry members point out that shark incidents have increased and fatalities have occurred. According to the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, at least one in four fishing trips now result in sharks biting off portions of the catch.

The diving industry emphasizes that shark tourism generates both economic and conservation benefits for coastal communities. These operations provide therapeutic and recreational experiences while raising public awareness about ocean conservation. Campbell has already sent a letter to Congress urging senators to delay action, commission research, and include all stakeholders, including both tourism operators and fisheries, in developing any new regulations. Campbell stated the industry is "not scared of accountability" and simply wants the chance to prove their position using science-backed evidence rather than having regulations based on what he calls "knee-jerk reactions and fear."

hero.headline: Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties face millions in losses under proposed property tax referendum
hero.teaser: A new property tax reform referendum would cost Martin County $50 million in 2027-28, St. Lucie County $80 million and Indian River County $32 million, according to a Florida Association of Counties study.
hero.body:
Government officials are working to assess the impact of the new property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills. A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties estimated Martin County would lose $50 million in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29. St. Lucie County would lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29. Indian River County would lose $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said if there is a cut to property taxes, there will be real shortfalls, real challenges and revenue will have to be made up somewhere. Powell said options like finding new revenue and budget cuts are a possibility but added that officials do not yet know if it will be an increase in sales tax, an increase in user fees for other services or something else. The referendum to raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 will be decided by voters in November. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the proposal is more of a break for the struggling family in a $300,000 home working several jobs to make sure ends meet.

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway to make way for 300,000-square-foot mixed-use development in Vero Beach
cards.teaser: Crews began demolition this week on portions of the Indian River Mall in Vero Beach as part of a revitalization project for the shopping center.
cards.body:
Crews began demolishing portions of the Indian River Mall this week as part of a revitalization project. Joseph Scarfone, the project manager for the redevelopment, said crews are working on the first phase by taking down Macy's and soon the former Sears location. Neighbors gathered in the parking lot to watch the demolition unfold.

Mary Alice Stopyra, a neighbor, expressed support for the demolition, saying the mall "has degraded over time." Mark Manera from Vero Beach offered a different perspective, calling it "the death of a beautiful building" and describing how he has watched "a steady decline year after year." Despite his nostalgia, Manera said if the new project brings "new life, new jobs, new opportunity, that's wonderful." Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a new sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center with around 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants and possible residential spaces. He described it as "a city within a city," noting residents will no longer see "a dead mall for the last 12 years that was getting cobwebs." Scarfone hopes the first phase can be completed by 2027, while the project team continues working on permitting for the rest of the development.

The 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report found Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. According to the report, the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site, is already half lost to erosion. Wildlife refuges like Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park are also threatened. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town continues to fight erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project. Field said the town is reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and will continue to do that as long as there is money to do it. About $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment every year.

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup and Walmart over alleged worms in SpaghettiOs

cards.body:

The lawsuit seeks $50,000 in damages and alleges the companies failed to properly inspect the product. Campbell said the claims lack merit, while Walmart said it is reviewing the court filing.

hero.headline: Florida voters split on property tax proposal ahead of November vote
hero.teaser: Florida voters will decide in November whether to roll back property taxes by raising the homestead exemption for homeowners, a proposal drawing mixed reactions from residents in West Palm Beach.
hero.body:
Florida residents will vote this November on whether to increase the homestead exemption, effectively reducing property taxes for homeowners across the state. The proposal requires 60% voter approval to pass, the same threshold that caused a similar measure to fail in 2018. As the election approaches, West Palm Beach residents are expressing sharply divided opinions about whether the tax cut is a sound policy decision.

Supporters of the measure argue it benefits people who permanently reside in Florida as homeowners. Brian Edington, a local resident, said "I think it's a really good idea because it saves the people that really live in Florida, the homeowners." Edington expressed comfort with local governments spending less money and suggested that some services could be reduced without harming quality of life. He pointed to trash collection in his neighborhood as an example, noting that twice-weekly pickup could be scaled back to once weekly without negative effects. Another resident named Stan acknowledged potential concerns about budget cuts but suggested that modest reductions might be acceptable if they provide relief to residents.

Critics worry that reducing government funding could have serious consequences for essential services. Rosabella Olivares expressed concern about what lower revenues might mean for municipalities. "There's going to be less money ... because everything is expensive now," she said. The exact amount cities and counties would lose under the plan remains unclear, and officials have not determined where budget cuts would fall if voters approve the measure. Some residents questioned whether a services-based tax system might be more fair, suggesting people should only pay for services they directly use rather than supporting all government functions through property taxes.

Renters were particularly skeptical about the proposal's benefits. While homeowners generally supported paying lower taxes, renters noted they would likely not gain from the tax cuts since they do not own property. One downtown West Palm Beach renter predicted that landlords would pass along any tax savings to tenants through higher rents rather than sharing the benefits. "Pretty sure they're going to raise the rent on everybody, all the renters," the resident said. This concern highlights how the measure would affect different groups of Floridians differently, with homeowners potentially benefiting while renters and others who do not own property might see little advantage.

cards.headline: Martin, St. Lucie, Indian River counties face millions in property tax losses under Florida referendum
cards.teaser: Government officials across the Treasure Coast are working to assess the impact of a new property tax reform referendum that Florida voters will decide in Novem.
cards.body:
Government officials across the Treasure Coast are assessing the impact of a property tax reform referendum that Florida voters will decide in November. The measure would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills for homeowners. A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties estimated potential losses for the region: Martin County faces $50 million in losses in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29; St. Lucie County would lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29; Indian River County faces $32 million in losses in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29. Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said options like finding new revenue and budget cuts are possible. "If there's a cut when it comes to property taxes, there's going to be some real shortfalls, some real challenges and some revenue is going to have to be made up somewhere," Powell said. He noted the county is working with the Office of Management and Budget to determine the impact.

The referendum would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 and requires 60 percent approval to pass. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the proposal provides relief for families in $300,000 homes working multiple jobs to make ends meet. The savings for homeowners can vary from hundreds to thousands of dollars depending on the county, city and assessed home value.

cards.headline: 35 foster youth graduate at ChildNet celebration at Palm Beach State College
cards.teaser: 35 students walked across the stage at ChildNet's annual graduation celebration at Palm Beach State College, marking a milestone for foster youth and young adults served by the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit.
cards.body:
ChildNet celebrated 35 foster youth and young adults at its annual graduation ceremony at Palm Beach State College, marking a significant milestone for the Broward and Palm Beach County nonprofit. The organization supports foster children and young adults through education, adoptions and independent living resources. Among the graduates were Sabrina Diaz and Brian Saintfort, both of whom lost a parent and relied on ChildNet for support during their journey forward.

Diaz encouraged others facing similar circumstances, saying "Belief that you're going to be big one day and just put effort into it, never give up on school and never give up on dreams. If you like push past with the pain and just keep trying hard." Saintfort shared similar advice, stating "Believe that you'll make it, then you're gonna make it and stuff." Larry N. Rein, CEO of ChildNet, noted the evening represented "the fruition of great work by everyone in the community, including case workers at ChildNet, DCF and especially the kids who have worked so hard." Diaz is enrolled in pre-med classes at Palm Beach State College with aspirations to become a doctor, while Saintfort plans to pursue a vocational program to become a plumber.

hero.headline: 100 Paddlers to Cross 80 Miles of Ocean from Bimini to Lake Worth Beach for Cystic Fibrosis
hero.teaser: More than 100 paddlers will launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13 and paddle 80 miles across the open Atlantic Ocean to Lake Worth Beach in a 12 to 16 hour endurance trek benefiting families living with cystic fibrosis.
hero.body:
More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of the open Atlantic Ocean this June to raise awareness and funds for families living with cystic fibrosis in the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis. According to event founder Travis Suit, participants will launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13, arriving at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. The endurance trek benefits the Pipers Angels Foundation, which Suit established in honor of his daughter, Piper, diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4.

The crossing is part of a four-day schedule beginning June 10 with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. On Thursday, participants take part in a 4Ocean beach cleanup and a community buffet dinner. Friday brings a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony to honor cystic fibrosis warriors, followed by rest and safety checks before launch night. All paddlers are required to wear a U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation device, waterproof whistle, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers provided by the event must be worn and active at all times, and mandatory safety meetings will be held.

Paddlers must raise at least $2,000 for the cause, and crew or virtual participants have a $500 minimum. Final contributions are due July 31. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 to cheer paddlers during a daylong beach celebration marking their arrival. More information, registration, and donation details are available at crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

cards.headline: Broadway's 'Beetlejuice' Musical Playing at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach Through June 7
cards.body:
Broadway's "Beetlejuice" musical has arrived at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach, running June 2 through June 7 at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall. Actor Ryan Stajmiger plays the mischievous demon from Tim Burton's 1988 film, a character who appeared for only 15 minutes in the original movie but became iconic through Michael Keaton's performance. "I've loved the movie since I was a kid. I'm a huge Tim Burton fan, and you know, Michael Keaton's performance is so iconic," Stajmiger told WPTV. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a "strange and unusual" teenager whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble.

One of Stajmiger's favorite aspects of performing is breaking the fourth wall to communicate directly with the audience. "I get to break the fourth wall a lot, so I get to communicate directly to the audience and share some moments with them. That's my favorite part of theater," he explained, adding "That can go awry too." Early in the run, Stajmiger experienced an unexpected wardrobe malfunction when his second wig came off along with the first, leaving him bald for an entire scene. Rather than breaking character, he embraced the moment. "I got to play with that a little bit, and got to experience everyone seeing me for the first time and not knowing that I am bald." Performances run through June 7 with tickets starting at $34.50 at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up.

hero.headline: Donalds calls for GOP unity in Florida governor's race as opponents demand debates
hero.teaser: Byron Donalds is calling for the Republican party to unite behind his gubernatorial campaign more than two months before the August 18 primary, while opponents Jay Collins and Paul Renner demand he participate in debates.
hero.body:
Byron Donalds is calling on Republicans to unite behind his candidacy for Florida governor, arguing that the party should coalesce around him more than two months before the August primary election. The Naples Republican made this pitch for party unity on Friday, following Democrat Jerry Demings' announcement that he was withdrawing from the gubernatorial race due to a prostate cancer diagnosis. With Demings' departure, Donalds said "the general election starts today," signaling his view that the Democratic side is effectively settled with a presumptive nominee. He has raised $81 million to date and indicated he would prefer to spend those resources in the general election rather than continue competing in the Republican primary.

Donalds is positioning himself as the clear frontrunner based on his fundraising advantage and polling strength. He cites a "complete and total endorsement" from President Donald Trump and notes he leads by more than 40 points in multiple public polls. He argues that his opponents have not demonstrated comparable strength, with all other candidates polling in single digits. Donalds also contrasted his vision with that of Democrat David Jolly, saying their differences are stark and that Jolly would undermine Florida's appeal to people fleeing blue state governance. Donalds pledged to continue engaging voters through town halls, community meetings, business roundtables, and direct door-to-door canvassing, but notably refused to commit to participating in debates.

His opponents are pushing back against his debate avoidance. Jay Collins launched a website called The Collins Callout on Friday with messaging that acknowledges Donalds as the prohibitive frontrunner while challenging him to face off on stage. Former House Speaker Paul Renner went further, posting a video on social media in which he called out both Collins and Donalds for refusing to debate. "Floridians deserve to see the differences between the candidates. Stop ducking and let's get on stage," Renner said in his video appeal.

The financial picture shows a significant disparity among the Republican candidates. Through the end of March, Renner had raised more than $6 million and Collins approximately $1.75 million, according to the most recent available reports. Both candidates are expected to file updated fundraising reports covering activity through May on June 10, which should provide additional insight into the strength of their campaigns heading into the final stretch before the primary election.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds receives death threats during Florida gubernatorial campaign, calls for responsible political rhetoric
cards.teaser: Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds disclosed Friday that he has received multiple death threats while running for the Republican nomination in the Au.
cards.body:
Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds is speaking out about threats on his life as he runs for the Republican nomination in the August primary. The Naples Republican, in his third term in Congress, faced one threat on social media last month after resharing President Donald Trump's endorsement in the governor's race. A second person called Donalds' district office making similar threats, saying he was going to blow up the entire office. "Somebody just flat out said they were going to kill me," Donalds told radio host Mark Levin on Friday.

Donalds cited the assassination of conservative Charlie Kirk last year as an example of what happens when political opponents are demonized and not treated as human beings. He said that demonizing someone to the point where they are portrayed as going to destroy Florida gives an opening to somebody with real mental health issues to attempt violence. While considering himself a free speech absolutist, Donalds stressed the importance of being mindful of how things are being said to avoid creating an environment where someone takes it upon themselves to take another person's life. Donalds said the incident strengthened his resolve to work hard to be the state's next governor and to keep Florida free as the preeminent conservative and common sense state in America. He remains undeterred by the threats and expresses confidence in his position in the race to succeed Ron DeSantis.

cards.headline: Former Cuba President Raul Castro makes first public appearance since US murder indictment
cards.teaser: Raul Castro appeared in public for the first time since being indicted by the United States for his alleged role in the 1996 downing of two civilian aircraft, celebrating his 95th birthday with top officials and military leaders in Havana.
cards.body:
Raúl Castro made his first public appearance since being indicted by the United States for his alleged role in the 1996 downing of two civilian aircraft. Castro's celebration of his 95th birthday took place late Friday at the Ministry of Interior in Havana with top officials and military leaders. State TV broadcast footage showed Castro, clad in his olive-green military uniform, entering a packed theater to a standing ovation, followed by his grandson and bodyguard Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez and Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel.

Díaz-Canel delivered a tribute to the "heroism and dignity" displayed by Castro and his late brother Fidel Castro, praising Raúl Castro, who served as defense minister of Cuba for nearly 50 years, for his "courage and loyalty (that) made him a target from a very early age for the intelligence services of our enemies." The celebration offered Cuba's socialist government an opportunity to close ranks and project defiance as the Trump administration escalates its pressure campaign on the fuel-starved island. The Justice Department's indictment unsealed in May accuses Castro of ordering the 1996 shootdown of civilian planes flown by Miami-based exiles. Although he formally retired from politics in April 2021, Castro is believed to wield considerable political power.

cards.headline: Former Lake County Property Appraiser Carey Baker enters race for Florida's 11th Congressional District
cards.teaser: Carey Baker is running to succeed retiring U.S. Rep. Daniel Webster in Florida's 11th Congressional District, setting up a GOP Primary with Lake County Commissioner Anthony Sabatini.
cards.body:
The 63-year-old Baker represented much of the Central Florida district in Florida's Legislature, in both the House and Senate, before being elected countywide as a constitutional officer. Baker, a lifelong resident of Eustis, most recently served multiple terms as Property Appraiser. He lost re-election in 2024 after filing for re-election as a write-in candidate. After David Jordan filed as Republican, he defeated Baker by a 3-to-1 margin in the General Election. Baker is poised for a GOP Primary with Lake County Commissioner Anthony Sabatini, a onetime protégé who has already run for the seat.

Despite not winning the race for re-election, Baker demonstrated fundraising prowess that will come in handy in the race for the nomination, raising $233,000 for the campaign. After the latest round of Congressional redistricting, Florida's 11th Congressional District includes all of Sumter County, some of west Orange County and most of Lake County. Baker has remained a high-profile Republican leader in Lake County since his election to the Florida House in 2000 before he ascended to the Florida Senate. His father also served the area in the Florida House. CD 11 is likely to be Republican in November, with more than 57% of voters there backing President Donald Trump in the 2024 Presidential Election.

cards.headline: Democrat Benjamin Sandlin launches second bid for Jacksonville's HD 12
cards.teaser: Benjamin Sandlin filed Friday for a second run in Jacksonville's HD 12, where he lost by 14 points to House Speaker Pro Tempore Wyman Duggan two years ago. The seat is open because Duggan is term-limited.
cards.body:
Democrat Benjamin Sandlin is launching a second run in Jacksonville's HD 12, where he lost by 14 points to House Speaker Pro Tempore Wyman Duggan two years ago. The 22-year-old repeat candidate filed for the House race Friday, just three days before the beginning of qualifying on Monday, June 8. He said the Florida Democratic Party and he had been talking and that they agreed that this seat was just too close in 2024 to leave uncontested. "That'd be a huge missed opportunity to have an extra voice for labor rights, public schools and housing justice in the Legislature," Sandlin told Florida Politics on Saturday morning. As the sole Democrat in HD 12, it is likely Sandlin will advance to the November ballot upon qualifying.

Former Jacksonville City Council President Terrance Freeman is running in HD 12 to succeed Duggan in the open Republican-leaning seat. Freeman is well-positioned for his primary, having raised more than $167,000 to his campaign account and an additional $506,000 to an affiliated political committee called For the Future We Want through the end of May. He had roughly $390,000 on hand at the end of last month. Freeman was appointed to the Jacksonville City Council in 2018 by former Gov. Rick Scott to fill a vacancy and was then elected to an at-large, countywide seat twice in 2019 and 2023, serving a year as Council President.

cards.headline: Gatorland opens new craft beer bar featuring exclusive brew from Crooked Can Brewery
cards.teaser: Gatorland opened the Guzzlin Gator Beverage Barn on Memorial Day Weekend and is selling an exclusive craft beer made by Crooked Can Brewery that can only be found at the Orlando park.
cards.body:
Gatorland celebrated the start of summer by opening the Guzzlin' Gator Beverage Barn on Memorial Day Weekend, an outdoor, shaded bar near the Legends of the Swamp show. The new craft beer hub features the Grinnin' Gator lager, an exclusive brew made by Crooked Can Brewery that can only be found at the park. The bar serves the Grinnin' Gator on tap along with five other pours, including offerings from Orlando's Ivanhoe Park and Orange Blossom breweries. Additional drinks are available in cans. Gatorland's Director of Food and Beverage Tim Acheson described the space as a place for guests to relax in the heat, reflecting the park's "old Florida" philosophy of taking it easy and enjoying the day.

Crooked Can Brewery, located in Winter Gardens, settled on a Pale German lager with hints of citrus after Acheson approached the brewery for help developing a specialty beer. "Ultimately we wanted to provide a beer that was kind of a beer for everybody, which is why we landed on that pale lager," said Alan Delahunt, Managing Partner at Crooked Can Brewing Company. Acheson called it a "summertime sipper" with notes of grapefruit and orange peel. The Grinnin' Gator is currently served in plastic cups, but Gatorland plans to sell six-packs with decorative cans in the gift shop. Acheson teased that additional beer collaborations are in development at the park.

cards.headline: Sen. Rick Scott remembers father's D-Day service on 82nd anniversary
cards.teaser: Sen. Rick Scott honored the memory of his father Orba Scott, who parachuted behind enemy lines during the D-Day operation in 1944, on the 82nd anniversary of the military operation.
cards.body:
On Saturday, Naples Republican and Navy veteran Sen. Rick Scott remembered what many members of the military endured on D-Day, the famous 1944 World War II military operation in which more than 160,000 Allied troops stormed the beaches of Normandy and made first headway in the liberation of German-occupied France. Orba Scott, who raised the Senator, was among those engaged in the operation. As the Senator recounts, his adopted father parachuted behind enemy lines and selflessly fought for the well-being and freedom of Americans and families across the world.

"My father was blessed enough to return home from battle, but many brave individuals made the last full measure of devotion in defense of freedom and didn't return home," Sen. Scott said. As a Navy veteran and the son of an Army veteran, Scott vowed to continue fighting for those who have fought for America. "I am fighting every day to improve our military, take care of our nation's veterans, and protect your legacy so the next generation knows and appreciate the sacrifices made for their freedoms," he said.

hero.headline: Summer fertilizer ban begins June 1 in Martin County
hero.body:
Starting June 1, Martin County residents must stop using fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen on their lawns and landscaping. The restriction lasts through September 30. Indian River and St. Lucie counties have adopted the same ban during this four-month period. Anyone using fertilizer products during these months needs to check ingredient labels carefully and avoid any products listing these two nutrients.

The ban exists to address a significant environmental concern. During Florida's rainy season, nutrient-rich fertilizer runoff flows into local waterways and can trigger algae blooms. These blooms damage ecosystems like the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. Jordan Skaggs, with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, explained that algae can shade out the beneficial plants that fish and wildlife depend on for survival. When harmful algae blooms reach certain densities, they can release toxins that threaten human health, harm wildlife, and damage the overall health of the ecosystem.

For residents concerned about maintaining their gardens and landscaping during the ban, composting offers a practical alternative. Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as an effective way to add nutrients to landscapes without breaking the rules. According to Ricketts, setting up a composting system can be simple and affordable. A small trash can works as an easy and practical option for those looking to maintain their landscape during the restriction period.

The seasonal fertilizer restriction applies uniformly across all three Treasure Coast counties and remains in effect through the end of September. Residents who regularly fertilize their lawns should plan ahead and either use up their current fertilizer supplies before June 1 or switch to alternative methods like composting for the summer months. Understanding the ingredients in any fertilizer products is essential, as any product containing phosphorus or nitrogen violates the ban, regardless of the product type or brand.

hero.headline: Summer fertilizer ban begins June 1 in St. Lucie, Martin, and Indian River counties
hero.body:
Starting June 1, residents in Indian River, Martin, and St. Lucie counties will need to stop applying fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen. The restriction continues through September 30, covering the region's rainy season when nutrient runoff poses the greatest environmental risk.

The ban exists to address a serious water quality problem. Jordan Skaggs, with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, explained that the prohibition reduces nutrient-rich runoff during the wet months, which is a major factor in triggering algae blooms. These blooms damage important waterways including the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River, creating ecological disruptions throughout the region.

The consequences of unchecked algae growth extend beyond cloudy water. According to Skaggs, the blooms "can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife." More concerning, certain types of algae blooms can become toxic at high concentrations. "At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that can affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health," Skaggs noted. These toxins create risks for people who use the waterways and for the animals that depend on them for survival.

For those maintaining gardens and landscapes during the ban period, composting offers a practical solution. Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommended composting as an effective alternative. According to Ricketts, a compost system functions simply and can be as basic as "a small trash can." He emphasized that composting provides "the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape" while complying with the summer restrictions.
